stem: An officer says torturing a detainee is allowed because the country faces a threat of war. Under RA 9745 (the Anti-Torture Act of 2009), is he right?
choices: Yes, but only while a state of war exists.
Yes, if the detainee is named in an order of battle.
No. A threat of war can never justify torture.
No, unless a superior officer gave the order.
answer: No. A threat of war can never justify torture.
hints: The officer points to an emergency as an excuse. Check whether RA 9745 allows any excuse at all.
Recall Section 6 of RA 9745. Its title calls freedom from torture an absolute right.

Section 6 lists things that "shall not and can never be invoked" to justify torture. See whether war, a threat of war or an order of battle is on that list. Then recall what Section 13 says about a superior's order.

solution.methodName: Match the situation to the provision

steps.action: Spot the excuse: a threat of war.
Find the provision: RA 9745, Section 6, which makes freedom from torture an absolute right.
steps.why: Absolute means it has no exceptions.

steps.action: Section 6 says: "A state of war or a threat of war, internal political instability, or any other public emergency, or a document or any determination comprising an 'order of battle' shall not and can never be invoked as a justification for torture".
steps.why: So war, a threat of war, emergencies and an order of battle are all ruled out as excuses.

steps.action: Section 13 makes anyone who "actually participated" in torture liable as a principal, and a superior who ordered it "equally liable". So an order is no excuse either.
The answer is: No. A threat of war can never justify torture.
